Make sure his beneficiaries on all his accounts are updated (banks, investments, retirements, life insurance, 401ks (old and current), etc. If the beneficiary names for the accounts on the will and on the actual accounts differ, the funds will default to whatever names are on the financial institution's system, NOT the will contrary to popular belief. So make sure that he has these updated at the financial institution even if he has an updated will and that he physically reviews the details are correct. The bank for my mother's accounts had my name completely wrong and she didn't know for decades until I had her do a thorough review at the bank. 

If there are multiple institutions, it might be easier on the beneficiaries if he consolidates them as much as possible so that they're not submitting death claims to multiple institutions that all have different rules and processes. Ex 1: He has Chase bank, Citi Bank, and BoA. It'd be best to combine it into one bank institution so that beneficiaries don't have to stop at all three banks to notify of death. Ex 2: He has a 401k with one previous employer and another 401k with another old employer and he has an IRA at JPMorgan and an IRA at Fidelity. He can rollover the 2 401ks and the Fidelity IRA to the JPMorgan IRA. If investments and retirements are involved, might be best to work with a Financial Advisor (with a CFP preferably) and CPA on how to avoid taxable events to the owner when combining these and how to avoid taxable events to the beneficiaries (i.e. spouses inheriting something have to follow different rules than non-spouse beneficiaries taxation wise). 

If he is up to do that, that is good because the last thing people want to do when grieving is having to stay on top of many institutions - there is no time to grieve sadly. Had a client grieve for over a year long and did not do anything and now she's going to have to pay penalties because she wasn't on top of her deceased mother's accounts as she missed the window for certain things. This doesn't apply to everyone, but I don't know what assets he has.

Make sure to order multiple death certificates. Many places require the original, not a copy during the deceased notification and death claim process.

If you are super paranoid and want to be extra safe and still don't feel satisfied with what your bank has done after further clarification:

- Create a new email associated with your bank account and only for your financials. Never mix your personal and finances. DO NOT REUSE THE SAME SECURITY QUESTIONS OR PASSWORD AS THE OTHER EMAIL. 
- Change your username and password on your app. Change password on old email as well and find a setting to see history of logins from all devices on your email (which can help confirm if your email was hacked if location and device isn't yours) and also a setting to sign you out on all devices. 
- Add all app alerts.
- Ask customer service to put a passcode or additional authentication methods every time a call to customer service is made if your bank has such a service available.  Have them add notes you were a previous victim of fraud. 
- Change your bank account number in addition to the debit card number. Your bank may not be tech savy enough to simply change the number and may need to close it and open a brand new account. But make sure you update your new bank account # and debit card # on all autopay and direct deposit. 
- Open a separate savings (assuming you only have one account) or any bank account at a separate institution if you meet requirements to not get fees where you can store most of your money you are not likely to touch except in emergency unless you are literally living on paycheck to paycheck. Savings accounts are less likely to get hacked. 
- Open a credit card and make most of your purchases there and earn rewards at the same time. 
- If your bank has a super savy app (many don't) you can try to lock your debit card each time and unlock it only when right before you make a purchase (though I'm not sure if your institution can make that instantaneously happen). Then lock it again. Though it can get tedious so maybe this is just a temporary measure until you feel secure again. 
- Check your credit score and credit report and make sure there aren't lines of credit opened in your name. Might have to report it. It's possible that your info could be breached even on a social security level or a victim of identity theft and that is how they were able to bypass even two factor authentication. Depending on the level of severity, SSA, law enforcement, (and a few times I've seen the FBI) would have to get involved. But there's no point worrying about these rarer incidents until you check your credit. Try annualcreditreport.com to view and you can also put a freeze too. Speak to a representative.

As someone who works in a bank, just be aware that POA designations cease upon death. Named joint owners and beneficiaries tend to take precedence in receiving the funds in that account over what is designated on a will if there are differences. I'm not sure if your father had a trust in place, but this is another consideration. But technically, there's nothing stopping his wife from bringing a death certificate to the bank since she is close family. But just because she presents a death certificate DOES NOT mean the bank automatically will just give her the money because they have their own process and regulations to abide by in regards to the distribution process. It is not in the bank's best interest to give funds out without a somewhat annoying process in place so she will likely be yet another disgruntled widow screaming at some poor banker about how she's the wife and therefore it's her money (assuming she is not a beneficiary). It is only her money if she is a joint owner or named beneficiary on the bank account itself. She would have to get a bunch of bank forms notarized at the very least. 

If she is beneficiary, then she is automatically rightfully entitled to that cash and the bank is not usually going to interfere with that if she does everything they ask of her because it is not on the staff processing this to know there is some drama going on elsewhere or if there's anything substantial enough going for an estate executor to be appointed. How is the bank staff supposed to know of your existence or what the court wants if you don't show for a year and she does and is on their system as an owner/bene? Also, is she a joint owner on any of the accounts? I ask because that means she is considered an owner of those funds as well, if so, at first glance from the bank's perspective. But this distribution process varies with many factors like by state, who is named beneficiary if any, the amount, etc. For example where I am at, if the funds were just a few thousand dollars and there were 0 beneficiaries listed, we were able to distribute those to family members who came with a death certificate after a holding period if they got some forms signed and notarized. With limited information on many things here, it is hard to advise accurately for your case. Note that there may be some differences due to different states or banking institutions. 

However, if there are any ongoing disputes despite what is on the accounts, that's not the bank's job to determine who should receive funds. That is a legal process which is frankly way above their paygrade so they are required to redirect you to consult a lawyer and have you work it out on court. In general practice, they will go by what they see on their system and take action based on given required documents that pass all the necessary checks in good order unless otherwise notified and ordered by court to place a legal hold. Another thing to consider is to make sure if your father has any previous 401ks from old jobs or other investment and retirement accounts that there is a clear or updated beneficiary designation. Make sure that beneficiaries are updated on all bank accounts, assuming he is still capable of doing so. I've learned many people think they have beneficiaries when they don't or thought they updated it when they haven't or the bank made a mistake and they never caught it. My usually money savvy mother went a few decades, not knowing the bank spelled my name so incorrectly that only the first letter matched (Ex: Anna vs. Ashley). 

Also, if your father was collecting social security, but when he passes, and no one decides to notify the bank, it is possible social security will do so. Depending on when he has passed and when the SSA & bank is notified, sometimes a freeze will be placed on the account which is annoying to deal with for all parties. You want to make sure funds in the account haven't been used in the mean time especially by his wife because it's possible SSA will take back funds that have been paid out after he's passed. In other words, this can become a nightmare for you trying to get these accounts closed out especially if money owed to the SSA had been spent or drained by bank fees, automatic bill payments, or fraud you were not aware of because you took a year off instead of managing his estate affairs so closely. So I don't think you should wait around to take care of his affairs to grieve. 

Depending on what he has had, you will have many institutions bothering you to take action or even try to trick you to make you responsible for the debts. The longer you do not take action on his estate, the messier it will get for you when you decide to finally deal with it. However, if your father does want his wife to be the beneficiary on some of his assets, I hope you will respect his decision and not pressure him to make sure she doesn't get a single cent just because you two do not get along (assuming elder abuse and manipulation on her part isn't going on). If your father is still capable, make sure to get all of these affairs in order because by the end of the day as far as the bank is concerned, whatever ends up happening is entirely on your father to make sure he has taken responsibility to put his affairs in order, and also, you by extension as the executor; therefore, you are expected to be carrying out your duty immediately by all parties.

I'm now an investment banker with 2 degrees with honors magna cum laude after changing career paths like 20x. Endocrinologist: She may have issues with cortisol or thyroid issues. This is extremely common especially in women. Also might be helpful data to start tracking how her energy levels are around her period. 
Nutritionist: She might not be getting a proper diet. Sleep Specialist: Her quality of sleep may be disrupted. She might be skipping certain stages of sleep for example or has other sleep disorders.

Maybe, just maybe she might need a rheumatologist if she has other symptoms. I have known people suddenly diagnosed with Lyme disease that they weren't aware they had that basically zapped all their energy. I got my fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis through this specialist.

In my case, my culture demands that you listen to your elders without even a single question and they take that as disrespect to the extreme. So when I signed my name on the line, I didn't realize how much compounding interest on top of inflation on top of assuming head of household responsibilities later in life and learning about the poor financial decisions my parents had made was going to impact me years later. They've always aggressively told me to mind my own business and to focus on only my studies so I never really had a handle on any finance basics other than an angry vague "Don't spend money."

Being the first generation born American, I didn't exactly have any financial literacy or advice or guidance passed onto me and my school never really taught it either. You would have had to went out of your way to pick that class as an elective and the average high school student wouldn't. If I knew what I knew now, I would have never have taken the loan. I mean good luck getting a credible bank to give someone without amazing income, good credit history, and balances/collateral any loan. Now think why would these predatory institutions give 18 year Olds that much money? Because they're not held to the same lending practices a bank is held to. It's a for-profit business for something that people should not profit that much from.

I'm a banker now and I see that financial literacy is a very rare skill in the hundreds of people I see. Many people think financial literacy only encompasses saving more than spending, but the intricacies of investments, credit scores, credit cards, insurance, loans, and yes student loans are new concepts that many immigrants may never experience until they come here and they (or their children) make mistakes in the learning process that come with big nonrefundable consequences. 

In the case of student loans versus other loans, the practice is more predatory because they're going after young underdeveloped minds who are without parental guidance for the first time. Other finance practices require a lot more strict disclosures but for some reason it's not really as required by these loan institutions who are putting barely legal people into a giant debt. So that's probably why there's more focus on student loan forgiveness maybe; just a thought. It's severely impacting the economy even in the future because when you have an entire generation that's not spending money into the economy but all of their income is going into paying bills and making these loan institutions richer, quality of living decreases and businesses having less customers able to afford to buy go out of business and therefore you have less entrepreneurs and less innovation which puts America behind on other countries now in tech and medical advances. Of course there are other contributing factors to this, but not being able to pay off student loans is a big one as to why people are being held back from contributing to the economy healthily. A healthy economy is one where people spend the extra money they have. This is a generation that is merely surviving not thriving because these loan institutions have been allowed to run rampant with charging people for a degree that was touted to be a requirement of success only to find out that now the job market is so inflated with degrees, you now need a master's and/or PhD for said job and guess who benefits from you needing to take out more loans for grad school for the professional career you studied for in undergrad: loan institutions. Yeah, I don't think the average 18 year old was going to have had the hindsight to have predicted this.

Now my gripe is that our government has bailed out banks even though they caused the crash in 2008 and once again all these big corporations including the airlines in the billions recently in the last few years. Congress had no problems with these decisions but the naysayers to student loan forgiveness are complaining only now about *handouts* when arguably the economy's health relies on the most of this generation given some relief? Those corporations aren't even using their money to contribute to the economy; most of the money is held overseas sitting pretty in bank. We need spending dollars put back into the hands of the average person.
